title: The Second Screen
content:
One of the consistent friction points in working with AI coding agents is the permission bottleneck.

You kick off a long task — refactor this module, implement this feature, investigate why this test fails. The agent starts working. Then it hits a permission prompt. It needs to run a shell command. It needs to write a file. It's asking: is this okay?

If you're at your computer, you handle it in seconds. But the whole point of these tools is that you can start something and walk away. Go make coffee. Go to a meeting. Come back to progress.

Except the agent is sitting there, stopped, waiting, because it needed to ask and you weren't there.

---

The obvious solution is to approve everything upfront. Some workflows do this — developers set permissions to "allow all" and let the agent run freely. But that's a trust decision with real consequences. An agent with unrestricted execution can make mistakes that are hard to undo.

The better solution is a second screen.

Your phone is already always with you. The question is whether it can become a lightweight control panel for processes running on your machine.

---

This is what Maestro Remote aims to be. Not a full development environment on your phone — that's the wrong target. Just the decision surface.

A notification appears: "Claude Code wants to run a Bash command."
You see the command. You tap Yes or No.
The agent continues.

You're in the meeting. You approved the read operation from under the table in two seconds. The agent kept working. When you come back, more progress has been made than if you'd blocked it.

---

The design constraints for this are interesting.

The information density needs to be right. Too little context and you can't make an informed decision. Too much and you won't read it. The right amount is: tool type, the key argument (what command, what file), which project it's from.

Everything else is secondary.

You're making a snap judgment in two seconds. Give people exactly what they need for that judgment and nothing more.

---

There's also the latency question. A permission prompt that takes 30 seconds to reach you (because of polling delays, notification lag, etc.) is a much worse experience than one that arrives in under 2 seconds.

For local WiFi polling every 2 seconds, the worst case is 2 seconds. That's acceptable for most cases.

For push notifications, it's typically under 1 second even over cellular. That's better, but requires more infrastructure.

For now: 2 second polling is good enough. When it isn't, we'll upgrade.

---

The second screen isn't about doing more on your phone. It's about keeping processes moving when you're not at your desk.

That's a narrow but genuinely useful function.
